#9985. I built a background remover that runs 100% in the browser. Here's how I made it 7x faster

Most "free" background removers upload your photo to a server, run a model on a GPU, and then ask you to pay for the full-resolution download. I wanted the opposite: the photo never leaves your device, the download is full resolution, and there is no account.

So I built Remove de Fundo, a background remover where the AI model runs entirely in the browser. The first version worked, but on real phones it was slow enough that people left before seeing a result. This post is about what made it slow and what fixed it.

End result on the same laptop and the same photo: 43.8 s → 6.4 s from click to cutout.

Everything happens client-side. The server only serves static files.

The first visit downloads ~100 MB (model + ONNX runtime). That is unavoidable for an in-browser model, but I noticed something worse: the CDN serving the model sent no Cache-Control header, and the edge marked it cf-cache-status: DYNAMIC. So returning visitors were often downloading the model again, and nothing was cached near the user.

Fix: self-host the model files. A build script downloads the model chunks once and puts them in public/ai//, and the library is pointed there with publicPath. Since the chunk file names are content hashes, they can be cached forever:

Now a returning visitor loads the model from disk cache: zero network.

One gotcha: the chunk files have no extension, and both the dev server and the host treated extensionless paths as pages (404). Saving them as .bin and rewriting the names in resources.json fixed it.

Phones always use the WebAssembly path, so CPU speed matters most. ONNX Runtime Web can use multiple threads, but only if the page is cross-origin isolated, because threads need SharedArrayBuffer.

I used credentialless instead of require-corp so Google Fonts and analytics keep working without CORP headers. Browsers that don't support it simply ignore it, so nothing breaks there.

Result (CPU, model already loaded): 22.7 s → 7.9 s per photo. Almost 3x, from two lines of config.

After enabling isolation, inference got much faster but the total barely improved. I logged a timestamp for each stage and found this:

Encoding a 1200 × 800 PNG should take a fraction of a second. I measured canvas.convertToBlob() on an idle page:

So isolation itself was fine. The problem: the library sets the WASM thread count to navigator.hardwareConcurrency (all cores), and ONNX's worker threads keep spin-waiting after inference. They occupy every core, and the browser's own image-encoding threads starve.

Fix: cap the thread count before the library loads. I used ONNX Runtime's own default (half the cores, at most 4) on CPU, and 1 thread on the GPU path, where the GPU does the work:

Post-processing went from ~10 s back to 0.2 s.

On the WebGPU path, the second photo took 2 s but the first took ~17 s on every page load. The session creation and, mostly, the first inference compile the GPU shaders.

Fix: warm up on intent. When the user hovers the upload area (desktop) or taps it (mobile), I:

While the person is still picking a photo from their gallery, all of that is already happening. I skip the warm inference on CPU: on a phone it would take as long as a real cutout and the user's photo would wait behind it. I also skip prefetching on saveData or 2G connections, and on mobile only a tap on the upload box triggers it, so scrolling past doesn't burn 100 MB of someone's data.

Since adding analytics, about 98% of removals succeed and more than half of the people who upload a photo download the result.

The heavy lifting is done by IMG.LY's background-removal-js (AGPL-3.0) and ONNX Runtime Web. If you build something similar, check their licenses.

You can try it here: removedefundo.com/en. It's free, with no sign-up, and works in English, Spanish and Portuguese. I'd love feedback, especially from people on older phones.

This post was written with AI assistance. The numbers come from real measurements on the live site.

#9984. This fall, reach for this unlikely apple ingredient : Apple cider vinegar is a baker’s secret weapon.

As fall baking season settles in, you're probably reaching for apples — and the many flavor-packed ingredients they produce. Applesauce cooks down into tangy apple butter to be cradled in a flaky galette, while a drop of boiled cider can deliver supercharged apple flavor to crumb cake. But the baking ingredient you may be overlooking may be something you associate more with salad dressings and wellness tonics: apple cider vinegar.

This tangy, apple-y vinegar is a secret ingredient in some of our favorite fall recipes, including cookbook author Claire Saffitz’s Cinnamon-and-Sugar Apple Pie. While lemon juice is the standard acid used in most fruit pie fillings, Claire opts for apple cider vinegar here to complement the filling’s flavors. “It helps as a flavor enhancer, and I also like that it’s apple cider in an apple pie. It’s a nice symmetry,” she mentions.

Similarly, apple cider vinegar is used in the cooking liquid alongside sugar and butter to caramelize apples in a Classic Apple Tarte Tatin. The benefit is twofold: Vinegar’s acidity helps cut the sweetness of the caramel, and it prevents the apples from getting too mushy, instead maintaining their fork-tender texture.

Pastry chef and cookbook author Natasha Pickowicz often leans into the jolt vinegar can add, including adding a few drops to her cake soaks for an additional layer of flavor. “Cake soaks should have a balance of tart, sweet, and savory notes — just like vinaigrette for your favorite salad,” she writes in her cookbook More Than Cake. It can add intrigue to layered cakes like this Golden Spice Cake or Pumpkin Layer Cake. In her cookbook, she also calls for a glaze spiked with apple cider vinegar to brush onto an apple tart after baking. It’s the finishing touch “to further emphasize the tart’s resolute apple-ness,” she writes.

Apple cider vinegar doesn’t need to be limited to only apple desserts, either. In our Old-Fashioned Pecan Pie, we call for apple cider vinegar as a foil to the brown sugar filling’s cloying sweetness. A spoonful of apple cider vinegar may not announce itself boldly, but it makes a small splash for brighter, more balanced bakes.

#9982. Four Models in Seven Weeks. Benchmarks Are a Distraction.

Posted on Nov 21 • Originally published at computeleap.com

Google launched Gemini 4 Neon on November 18 — its fourth Gemini 4 model in seven weeks, priced at $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens. It debuted #1 on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index with a score of 58.6, scored 61 on the AA Intelligence Index at its highest thinking setting, and reportedly matched Claude Opus 5.5 on a real coding benchmark at less than half the cost per task.

📖 Read the full version with charts and embedded sources on ComputeLeap →

Those numbers matter. But they are not the story. The story is that the leaderboard has fractured so completely that four labs can each claim #1 on a different index — and that Google is using price, not performance, as the weapon that actually moves markets.

View original announcement on Google Blog →

Here is what Google shipped in the Gemini 4 family since late September:

That is a new model roughly every 12 days. No other lab has matched this shipping velocity in 2026. Anthropic's last major release was Claude Opus 5.5 on September 22 — nearly two months ago. OpenAI shipped GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol on November 17, the day before Neon, and the consensus across YouTube and Substack is that it "got slept on."

We covered the Carbon/Hydrogen double-launch last week. The pattern continues: Google is not trying to win one benchmark cycle. It is trying to make the benchmark cycle irrelevant by shipping faster than anyone can evaluate.

The benchmarks are close enough to argue about. The pricing is not.

Artificial Analysis measured the cost per Intelligence Index task across effort levels:

At the default settings that most developers actually use, Neon scores 60 at $3.74 per task. Claude Opus 5.5 scores 52 at $3.46. Neon delivers 15% more intelligence for 8% more money. At maximum effort, the gap widens — Neon hits 61 for $6.44 while Opus reaches 59 for $10.04. That is a 36% cost premium for two fewer index points.

The Neuron's cost analysis puts it even more starkly: on the Coding Agent Index, Neon in Google's Antigravity CLI costs $6.86 per task versus $15.47 for Claude Fable 5.2 in Claude Code. That is 56% cheaper for a one-point advantage on the coding index (59 vs 58).

💡 Google's pricing pattern is becoming clear: launch at an aggressive introductory rate, let developers build on it, then normalize upward. Argon and Carbon both started at $2/$10 and jump to $4/$20 on December 1. The question is whether Neon's $3/$15 is permanent or another intro hook.

The cached input rate — $0.15 per million tokens, a 95% discount — is where the subsidy becomes structural. For agentic workloads that repeatedly reference the same codebase or document context, effective input costs approach zero. This is not a competitive move against Claude's pricing. It is a competitive move against Claude's architecture.

Here is the uncomfortable truth that AI Explained laid out this week: every frontier lab can now claim #1 on something.

The scores are bunched so tightly that the leader changes with every new model drop. When we wrote about Argon winning 12 of 18 benchmarks but ranking 8th in Code Arena, the split was novel. Now that pattern is the norm — every model has blind spots, every model has crown jewels, and the benchmark table has become a marketing surface where labs highlight the rows where they win.

This is not a problem that more benchmarks solve. It is a structural feature of a market where three to four labs are within 2-3 percentage points of each other on most tasks. The meaningful differentiation has shifted from "which model is smartest" to "which model is cheapest for my specific workload" — and that is a question only your production data can answer.

The prediction markets are not confused. Polymarket's "best AI model end of 2026" has Google at 86% — up 44 percentage points this month alone. Anthropic sits at 10%. OpenAI is at 2%.

That 2% is the most striking number on the board. The market has effectively written OpenAI out of the frontier conversation for this cycle, despite Astra launching to what Sam Altman called "amazing" and "very token-efficient" models.

Meanwhile, the AI bubble burst timing market jumped 20% this week — the crowd pulling the pop date forward to mid-2027. This is happening in the same week as Anthropic's record $81.3B IPO. Classic late-cycle behavior: the biggest raise and the loudest bust predictions arriving simultaneously.

David Sacks frames the emerging narrative: Anthropic is "racing toward Recursive Self-Improvement faster than any other frontier lab" — and doing so with public market money and a quarterly clock. Google's response is not to race toward RSI. It is to make the existing intelligence tier so cheap that the race becomes economically irrelevant for most buyers.

The community reception splits along predictable lines.

On YouTube, TheAIGRID called Neon "the first real Opus 5.5 competitor for coding agents." Theo went further, calling it his favorite model. AI Explained's take was more measured — progress is real but domain-dependent, and no single model wins across all workloads.

On Reddit, r/ClaudeAI is simultaneously buzzing about the Anthropic IPO (2.2K upvotes) and a stealth model reportedly beating Fable 5.2 on the FDB leaderboard (1.3K upvotes). The juxtaposition is telling — the community is tracking both the financial narrative and the technical competition in the same breath.

The Substack coverage splits into two camps. The Neuron focused on cost analysis, concluding that the pricing gap is "the real story." Latent Space and AI Supremacy treated the week as an Anthropic story with Google as a subplot. Neither framing captures the full picture — this is a market structure story, not a single-company story.

⚠️ Contrarian Corner: The Subsidy Trap. Google's introductory pricing has a pattern: Argon and Carbon both launched at $2/$10 and jump to $4/$20 on December 1 — a 100% increase. If Neon follows the same trajectory, the $3/$15 rate becomes $6/$30 within weeks. Teams that optimize for today's Neon pricing may find themselves locked into a model whose cost advantage evaporates on a corporate calendar. The labs with the stickiest developer ecosystems — Claude Code, Cursor's integration with Anthropic — may win regardless of per-token cost, because switching costs compound faster than token savings.

Zoom out from any single model and the structure becomes clear. Google is running a periodic-table naming scheme that maps to pricing tiers: Hydrogen ($1.50 input) is the speed tier, Neon ($3) is the value tier, Carbon ($4 post-promo) is the premium tier, and Argon ($4) is the deep-reasoning tier. Each model occupies a price point, not just a capability band.

This is not how Anthropic or OpenAI think about their lineup. Anthropic has Haiku, Sonnet, Opus, and Fable — a good/better/best hierarchy. OpenAI has a Sol/Astra split. Google is building a periodic table where you pick the element that matches your budget constraint, not your intelligence requirement.

The implication: Google is competing on portfolio breadth, not peak performance. When every lab's best model scores within 2-3 points of the others, the lab with the most pricing options captures the most of the demand curve. The DeepSeek V4 Flash price collapse earlier this year showed that aggressive pricing can reshape market expectations overnight. Google appears to have absorbed that lesson.

Test Neon on your production workload before December. The $3/$15 rate may be introductory. Run your actual tasks — not benchmarks — through the Gemini API and compare cost-per-completion against your current provider. The cached input rate ($0.15/M tokens) makes repeat-context workloads dramatically cheaper.

Build model-agnostic harnesses. The leaderboard rotates monthly. If your agent workflow is hardcoded to one provider's API, you are paying a tax every time the leader changes. Abstract the model layer. The teams winning right now are the ones that can swap providers in a config file.

Watch the December 1 price reset. Argon and Carbon both jump to $4/$20 on December 1. If Neon stays at $3/$15 through the reset, it becomes the unambiguous value pick in Google's own lineup. If it jumps too, the cost advantage over Anthropic narrows significantly.

The frontier AI market in November 2026 looks less like a technology race and more like an airline pricing war. The planes are all roughly the same. The routes are all roughly the same. The question is who has the deepest pockets to subsidize fares until the other carriers blink — and who builds the loyalty program that keeps customers even after the sale ends.

Google has the deepest pockets. That is not a prediction. It is a balance sheet.

For our previous coverage of the Gemini 4 family, see How Google Out-Iterated the Entire Model Race and Gemini 4 Argon Wins 12 of 18 Benchmarks. Code Isn't One..

#9981. Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.

A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models. The full version will be on arXiv soon.

GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today. Anyone running a shared cluster has to decide, every day, which jobs go on which GPUs and in what order. That plan is only as good as the estimate of how long each job will take. When a job finishes hours early, GPUs sit idle until the next one is dispatched. When it runs hours late, everything queued behind it slips, experiments wait and delivery dates move.

Better duration estimates turn this into planning instead of guesswork: what runs, when, and on how many GPUs, with less idle capacity in between. Yet the estimate most teams use is a back-of-the-envelope FLOP calculation. It says nine hours, and the job finishes the next afternoon.

We wanted to know how far off that math really is, and whether we could do better before a job is even dispatched. So we took 272 real supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jobs from our production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total, and compared analytical estimates against learned predictors.

The short version: the usual FLOP-based estimate explains little of what we observed (R² = 0.31, MAE 12.41 h). A CatBoost regressor that only sees information available before dispatch reaches R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation. The gap comes from two things a closed-form estimate cannot do. The regressor sees more training-specific signals, such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime, and it learns the nonlinear interactions between them from past runs.

For a dense Transformer, training costs roughly 6·P·D floating-point operations, where P is the parameter count and D the number of training tokens. Divide that by what your GPUs can deliver and you get a training-loop time:

Here N_GPU is the number of GPUs, FLOPS_peak is the peak throughput of one GPU from its spec sheet, and MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) is the fraction of that peak the training actually achieves. Real jobs never run at peak because of memory traffic, communication and kernel inefficiencies, so MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance.

This is a good description of the optimization loop. A job is more than its loop, though. Before the first step there is environment setup, model download and loading, and tokenization. During training there are periodic evaluations and checkpoint uploads. At the end, the final model goes to object storage. On a multi-tenant cluster, all of it competes with other jobs for network and storage I/O.

These overheads depend on configuration, and they do not scale neatly with workload or GPU count. Two jobs with the same nominal compute can finish hours apart.

To keep the comparison fair, the FLOP baseline we test counts the scheduled evaluation tokens as well as the training tokens, and we sweep MFU over a wide range.

We treat end-to-end duration as a supervised regression problem. Given a feature vector built from the job configuration and model metadata, predict the wall-clock time between the moment the job gets its GPUs and the moment it is done. Queue time is excluded.

We compared Linear Regression, Ridge, XGBoost and CatBoost. Feature selection combined correlation filtering, mutual information and permutation importance across 18 candidate feature sets, followed by a grid search with MAE as the criterion. The final CatBoost model uses 24 features.

Distribution of end-to-end duration across the 272 runs. Mean 23.43 h, median 15.29 h.

All numbers come from stratified 5-fold cross-validation. The first four rows are analytical and involve no fitting.

No single MFU value fixes the FLOP baseline. We swept MFU from 0.25 to 0.65. The best setting, 30%, still leaves a mean error above 12 hours on jobs that last 23 hours on average.

A more detailed analytical model does not close the gap. As a second baseline we took Calculon (Isaev et al., SC '23), an analytical performance model for LLM training from prior work. It builds an explicit layer graph and accounts for compute, memory traffic and inter-device communication. We extended the public implementation to cover LoRA, grouped-query attention, fused attention, bfloat16 and SwiGLU. Its estimates still correspond to a median of only 11% of the observed wall-clock time. That says nothing against Calculon as a step-level tool, which is what it was designed for. It shows how much of a production job happens outside the optimization step.

Linear models help, and then stall. Ridge brings MAE down to 7.23 h. The relationship between configuration and duration is not well captured by a purely linear model.

Gradient boosting does the heavy lifting. CatBoost and XGBoost land within one standard deviation of each other on every metric. We carry CatBoost forward because it has the lowest mean error across the board.

CatBoost's feature importance concentrates in a handful of features. Model and workload variables are there, as expected, but so are evaluation and checkpoint variables. num_eval_data, the total number of samples processed in evaluation over the life of the job, ranks first, followed by num_trainable_params, batch_eval_size_percent, num_all_params and num_gpus*batch_train_percent, with num_params_saved close behind. SHAP values tell the same story: high evaluation volume consistently pushes the predicted time up, while trainable parameter count has a nonlinear effect that only becomes large for the biggest models.

Mean feature importance of the CatBoost model across folds (PredictionValuesChange).

Feature importance is not a causal claim. Still, the pattern lines up with how a job is actually spent. How often you evaluate, how large the evaluation set is and how many checkpoints you persist all shape the wall-clock time, alongside model and dataset scale. These are choices people often make by habit when writing a training config.

One caveat on reading the plots: larger GPU allocations show positive contributions to predicted time. In our data, bigger allocations go with bigger jobs, so num_gpus acts partly as a proxy for job scale. It does not mean adding GPUs makes a job slower.

Looking at all 272 out-of-fold predictions, the median absolute error is 0.51 h. 80% of predictions are within 2.20 h and 90% are within 4.31 h. Broken down by job duration:

Up to 60 hours, the median error stays at about one hour or less. The long tail is where the model struggles, and with only 13 runs above 60 hours we read that as a data limitation.

Out-of-fold absolute error against real duration, colored by duration range. Errors stay low up to 60 h and widen in the sparse tail.

More data should still help. On a fixed 20% holdout, MAE drops from 1.63 h to 1.50 h when going from 85% to 100% of the training partition, with no clear plateau.

In practice, the predictor gives a scheduler a duration it can plan around before a job starts: which jobs to run together, when GPUs will free up, and whether a run will finish in time for its deadline.

What does transfer is the method: overhead-aware features, multicollinearity-aware selection and the comparison protocol. The full paper will report the feature formulas, the selection procedure, the search spaces and the final hyperparameters in full, so the pipeline can be rebuilt on any execution-log dataset with a similar structure.

Next on our list: hardware-specific descriptors and validation on other GPU types, transfer learning for configurations with few observations, other training objectives, and more data on long runs.

The full paper is coming to arXiv soon. Follow the Dharma-AI organization on Hugging Face to be notified when it is out, and leave your questions in the comments below. We would like to hear how you estimate job duration on your own clusters.

#9980. Next.js DevIndicators and `appIsrStatus` in 2026: Reading Rendering Mode at a Glance During Development

Posted on Nov 21 • Originally published at jsmanifest.com

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Next.js 15.0 introduced appIsrStatus, a configuration option that displayed a small badge in the development viewport showing whether the current route rendered statically or dynamically. Next.js 15.2 deprecated that option and replaced it with a unified devIndicators API that consolidates rendering mode visibility, build activity status, and position control into a single configuration object. Next.js 16.0 removed appIsrStatus entirely. The on-screen indicator now appears by default in every Next.js project running in development mode, positioned at the bottom-left corner of the viewport, displaying a colored badge that reads "Static" or "Dynamic" based on how the framework rendered the route you are viewing.

This matters because the difference between static and dynamic rendering determines your application's performance ceiling. Static routes serve prerendered HTML from a CDN with single-digit millisecond response times. Dynamic routes execute server code on every request, adding 50-500ms depending on database queries, API calls, and compute regions. Teams that catch rendering mode regressions during local development prevent production incidents. Teams that ignore the indicator ship performance problems.

The appIsrStatus option appeared in Next.js 15.0 as a boolean flag. Setting appIsrStatus: true in next.config.js enabled a fixed-position badge that displayed the rendering mode for the active route. Developers could see whether their page rendered statically or dynamically, but they could not control where the badge appeared on screen. Projects with custom toolbars, debugging overlays, or accessibility widgets often found the indicator overlapping critical UI elements.

Next.js 15.2 introduced the position option as part of a broader devIndicators object. The same release deprecated appIsrStatus, buildActivity, and buildActivityPosition in favor of the unified structure. The new API accepts four corner positions: bottom-left, bottom-right, top-left, and top-right. The default remains bottom-left for backward compatibility with existing visual layouts.

Next.js 16.0 completed the transition by removing the deprecated options entirely. Any project still referencing appIsrStatus in its configuration file will encounter a build error instructing developers to migrate to devIndicators.position. The version history documents the migration path explicitly.

The consolidation reflects a broader pattern in Next.js development: collapsing multiple single-purpose configuration flags into structured objects that group related settings. The same principle applies to the images configuration, which moved from top-level imageSizes and deviceSizes arrays to a nested images object containing formats, deviceSizes, and imageSizes together.

For teams maintaining multiple Next.js versions, the migration path is straightforward. Projects on 15.0 or 15.1 can continue using appIsrStatus: true until they upgrade. Projects on 15.2 should migrate to devIndicators: { position: 'bottom-left' } to avoid deprecation warnings. Projects on 16.0 or later must use the new structure or the build will fail.

The indicator itself displays as a small rectangular badge with rounded corners, positioned absolutely within the viewport. The badge shows white text on a colored background: green for static routes, amber for dynamic routes. The color choice maps to the same visual language the framework uses in its CLI output during next build, where a green circle symbol marks static routes and an amber function symbol marks dynamic routes.

Next.js DevIndicator showing Static and Dynamic rendering modes in the browser viewport

The indicator execution flow starts when the Next.js development server renders a route. The framework determines whether the route will render statically or dynamically, then injects a small React component into the page that displays the badge with the appropriate label and color.

A route renders statically when it does not use request-time APIs and all data fetching operations cache their results. Static routes generate HTML at build time and serve the same content to every visitor. The framework can deploy these routes to a CDN with long cache durations because the content does not vary per request.

The indicator reads "Static" for routes that meet the static rendering criteria. This includes pages that fetch data using fetch() with caching enabled, pages that read from server-only modules without accessing request context, and pages that render purely from imported data or hardcoded constants. The green background signals that the route will serve from a CDN in production with minimal latency.

The indicator reads "Dynamic" for routes that opt out of static rendering. The amber background warns that the route will execute server code on every request, adding latency and increasing infrastructure costs. The warning does not mean the route is broken, but it does mean the performance profile has changed in a way that might violate your application's requirements.

Developers can verify the indicator's accuracy by running next build --debug and comparing the terminal output to the badge displayed during development. The build output uses a circle symbol for static routes and a function symbol for dynamic routes. The symbols appear next to each route path in a table that lists the entire application's route tree.

The debug output captures the framework's rendering decision at build time. The on-screen indicator reflects the same decision during development. Any mismatch between the two signals a problem in the developer's understanding of when routes opt out of static rendering.

The devIndicators configuration accepts two forms: a boolean or an object. Setting devIndicators: false disables the indicator entirely. Setting devIndicators: { position: 'bottom-right' } enables the indicator and places it in the specified corner.

The position option accepts four string literals. Each positions the badge in a fixed corner of the viewport with a small margin from the edges. The default value bottom-left matches the position most Next.js developers encountered when the indicator first appeared in 15.0. Teams with debugging tools, accessibility overlays, or custom development UIs in that corner should switch to bottom-right or one of the top positions.

Disabling the indicator requires setting devIndicators to false at the top level. This form takes precedence over the object form. A configuration that sets both devIndicators: false and devIndicators: { position: 'top-left' } will disable the indicator because the boolean form appears first in the TypeScript type hierarchy.

Disabling the indicator hides the visual badge but does not suppress build errors or runtime warnings. The framework continues logging rendering mode decisions to the terminal during development and displaying error overlays when a build fails. The indicator only controls the persistent on-screen badge that shows rendering mode for the current route.

Teams disable the indicator in three scenarios. First, when the visual badge conflicts with other development tools. Browser extensions, React DevTools overlays, and accessibility scanners often occupy the bottom corners of the viewport. Adding another fixed-position element creates visual clutter and makes it harder to click interactive debugging controls.

Second, when the indicator distracts during design reviews or stakeholder demos. Non-technical reviewers looking at a development build may ask questions about the badge that derail conversations about product features. Temporarily disabling the indicator for specific sessions keeps the focus on the work being reviewed.

Third, when the team has automated their rendering mode verification through other means. Projects that run next build --debug in continuous integration and fail the build when unexpected routes render dynamically do not need the on-screen indicator to catch regressions. The CI pipeline surfaces the same information earlier in the development cycle.

Most teams leave the indicator enabled. The visual feedback loop it provides catches mistakes faster than waiting for a build to complete. A developer adding a new route can see immediately whether their implementation stayed static or opted into dynamic rendering. That instant feedback prevents the common mistake of assuming a route renders statically when it actually executes server code on every request.

The official documentation recommends keeping the indicator enabled unless visual conflicts force you to disable it. The performance implications of accidental dynamic rendering justify the small amount of screen space the badge occupies.

The indicator reads the framework's rendering decision at development time, but several edge cases produce misleading results. The most common pitfall occurs when a route conditionally calls request-time APIs based on runtime logic the compiler cannot analyze statically.

The troubleshooting section explains this discrepancy: "If you expect a route to be static and the indicator has marked it as dynamic, it's likely the route has opted out of prerendering." The guidance assumes the indicator reflects production behavior accurately, but conditional logic breaks that assumption.

Teams catch this issue by running next build --debug before deploying. The build output shows whether routes render statically or dynamically based on the compiler's static analysis of the entire codebase. Any route that conditionally calls request-time APIs will appear as dynamic in the build output even if the development indicator showed static.

Another pitfall occurs with uncached data fetching. A route that calls fetch() without setting a cache option or revalidate value opts out of static rendering because the framework cannot prerender content that depends on external data sources without explicit caching instructions.

The indicator shows "Dynamic" for this route because the fetch call lacks caching configuration. Developers expecting static rendering need to add { cache: 'force-cache' } or { next: { revalidate: 3600 } } to the fetch options. The framework then caches the response and prerender the route at build time.

A third pitfall appears with dynamic route segments that use generateStaticParams(). Routes with dynamic segments like /posts/[slug] can render statically if the application provides the full list of valid slug values at build time. The indicator shows "Static" during development because the development server renders each request independently without checking whether generateStaticParams() covers all possible values.

Production builds fail if a user requests a slug not included in generateStaticParams() and the route does not export a dynamicParams configuration. The build succeeds but the route renders dynamically at runtime for unlisted slugs if dynamicParams is set to true. The indicator cannot predict this scenario because it evaluates each route in isolation without considering the interaction between static params and dynamic fallback behavior.

Teams avoid these pitfalls by treating the development indicator as a hint rather than a guarantee. The authoritative source of rendering mode information remains the next build --debug output. That output reflects the compiler's final decision after analyzing the entire application, including conditional branches, dynamic imports, and static param generation logic.

For projects requiring strict static rendering guarantees, the best practice is adding a post-build verification step that parses the debug output and fails the CI pipeline if any unexpected routes appear as dynamic. This approach catches rendering mode regressions before they reach production, regardless of what the development indicator displayed.

Build output showing static and dynamic route symbols in the terminal

Production debugging workflows that rely on rendering mode information use the next build --debug flag rather than the development indicator. The debug flag produces verbose output that includes the rendering decision for every route, the reason for dynamic opt-outs, and the specific APIs that triggered the decision.

Teams debugging unexpected rendering modes grep the build output for the route in question and read the reason provided by the compiler. The reason pinpoints the exact line of code that caused the opt-out. This information is more precise than the development indicator, which only shows whether the route rendered statically or dynamically without explaining why.

The debug output also surfaces routes that opted out of static rendering after the initial build analysis. Routes that call request-time APIs inside try-catch blocks, dynamic imports loaded after the initial render, or conditional branches that only execute in specific environments all appear as dynamic in the debug output even if the development indicator showed static.

Production incidents related to rendering mode typically manifest as latency spikes or increased infrastructure costs. A route that rendered statically in development but dynamically in production adds 100-300ms to response times because it executes server code instead of serving cached HTML. The team notices degraded performance metrics in their monitoring dashboard and investigates.

The first debugging step is comparing the development indicator's output to the production build logs. If the logs show a route rendering dynamically but the development indicator showed static, the team knows the issue stems from conditional logic or environment-specific code paths that only execute in production.

The second step is running next build --debug locally and searching for the route in question. The debug output explains why the route opted out. The team reads the reason, identifies the offending code, and decides whether to refactor the route to avoid the dynamic opt-out or accept the performance tradeoff.

For routes that must render dynamically, the team can improve performance by using loading.js or React Suspense boundaries to stream the response. Streaming sends the static shell of the page immediately while the server computes the dynamic portions. Users see content faster even though the route still executes server code on every request. This pattern appears in Next.js caching strategies and component-level rendering approaches.

Teams that catch rendering mode regressions during code review save hours of production debugging. The review process includes running next build --debug and comparing the output to the previous build. Any route that switched from static to dynamic triggers a discussion about whether the change is intentional. If it is unintentional, the team refactors the code before merging.

This workflow requires storing build artifacts in version control or a build cache. The team can diff the debug output from two builds and immediately see which routes changed rendering modes. CI pipelines automate this process by running the build, parsing the output, and posting a comment on pull requests showing which routes will render differently after the change merges.

The development indicator complements this workflow by providing instant feedback during local development. Developers see the rendering mode as they write code, catch obvious mistakes before committing, and avoid creating pull requests that fail the automated rendering mode checks. The combination of real-time feedback during development and automated verification during code review creates a defense-in-depth approach to preventing accidental dynamic rendering.

A team building an e-commerce platform adds a personalized recommendation section to their product detail pages. The recommendation engine queries a database using the current user's purchase history and browsing patterns. The developer implements the feature by calling a database client directly in the page component without caching the query results.

The development indicator switches from green "Static" to amber "Dynamic" as soon as the developer refreshes the page. The visual feedback prompts an immediate investigation. The developer realizes the uncached database query opts the entire route out of static rendering. They refactor the code to use fetch() with a 60-second revalidation period, which caches the query results and allows the route to render statically again. The indicator returns to green, confirming the fix worked.

Without the indicator, this mistake would have reached production. The product detail pages would have served 100-300ms slower because each request executes a database query instead of serving cached HTML. The team would have discovered the regression through monitoring alerts after users complained about slow page loads. The indicator caught the issue in seconds instead of hours.

Another team maintains a documentation site with hundreds of markdown pages. Each page renders statically at build time. A developer adds a "last updated" timestamp to the page footer by reading the file modification time from the filesystem during render. The filesystem access happens inside a server component that runs at build time for static routes but on every request for dynamic routes.

The indicator shows "Dynamic" after the change. The developer investigates and realizes filesystem access during render opts the route out of static prerendering because the Next.js compiler cannot guarantee filesystem stability across deployments. They refactor the code to read file modification times during the build phase and pass the timestamp as a prop to the component. The route renders statically again.

The indicator helps new team members understand which pages require server execution and which serve from a CDN. Onboarding documentation includes screenshots of the indicator showing the rendering mode for each major route. New developers learn the application's performance characteristics by looking at the badge as they navigate the site during local development.

These scenarios demonstrate the indicator's value as a development-time feedback mechanism. The amber "Dynamic" badge acts as a visual alert that prompts developers to investigate whether the rendering mode change was intentional. Most teams that adopt the indicator report catching 3-5 accidental dynamic rendering regressions per month during local development, before those regressions reach code review or production.

No. The devIndicators configuration only affects development mode. Production builds never include the indicator component regardless of the configuration value.

No. The indicator shows only "Static" or "Dynamic" in Next.js 16.0. Routes using Incremental Static Regeneration display "Static" because they prerender at build time. Routes using Partial Prerendering display "Dynamic" because they include dynamic segments that execute on every request.

The build command analyzes the entire application statically, including conditional branches and environment-specific code paths. The development indicator reflects only the code paths executed during the current development request. Conditional logic that changes behavior between development and production can produce different results.

No. The devIndicators configuration and on-screen badge only work with the App Router introduced in Next.js 13. Pages Router applications do not display rendering mode information during development.

No. The indicator uses fixed styling and displays only the two rendering modes Next.js recognizes: static and dynamic. Teams requiring custom rendering mode tracking need to build their own development tools using the Next.js compiler hooks.

The decision to keep the indicator enabled depends on two factors: whether visual conflicts force you to disable it and whether your team has automated rendering mode verification through other means. Teams without automated checks should keep the indicator enabled because it catches performance regressions faster than any other feedback mechanism. Teams with robust CI pipelines that parse next build --debug output can disable the indicator if the visual badge interferes with other development tools.

For most projects, the indicator provides more value than it costs. The small rectangular badge occupies minimal screen space and displays information critical to understanding application performance. The instant feedback loop prevents the common mistake of assuming a route renders statically when it actually executes server code on every request. That mistake costs hours of debugging time and creates production performance problems that affect real users.

The configuration is a single line in next.config.ts. Teams that find the indicator useful leave the default enabled. Teams that encounter visual conflicts change the position to an unused corner. Teams that explicitly prefer to verify rendering modes through build output rather than runtime indicators set devIndicators: false and add automated checks to their CI pipeline. The choice depends on team workflow and tooling preferences, not on the inherent value of the information the indicator provides. That information matters regardless of how you choose to surface it.

For more context on Next.js rendering modes and caching behavior, see Next.js Caching Mental Model 2026 and Next.js 16: Turbopack, Partial Prerendering, and Cache. Component-level rendering strategies that affect when routes opt into dynamic mode are covered in Next.js Dynamic IO and Component-Level Rendering.

#9979. DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency

Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles. We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks.

The checkpoints are available under Apache 2.0:

The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window. The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings.

We recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding. The SGLang cookbook provides launch configurations for different GPUs and checkpoint formats.

After starting the server with the served model name DaisyRose-27B on port 30000, you can send a request using the OpenAI Python client:

The model thinks before answering by default. Its reasoning is returned in reasoning_content, and its final answer in content. These settings follow the model card’s quickstart.

DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 rises from 5.6% to 12.0%.

Scores use the higher of the BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark; the two differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated. The model card includes comparison sources and evaluation settings.

Three parts of the training setup made this release possible: carefully designed tasks, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes.

We built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI, starting from its large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 made it into the final training set.

RadixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization.

57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU’s peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash.

2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs.

Stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady.

Every training step of the DaisyRose-27B release run on 144 H200s, plotted against total training time. Dashed lines: the open-source trainer on comparable runs.

Every training attempt runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task’s environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded.

Our service is built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, it ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running concurrently.

The service grew from one machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded; since late October, that figure has exceeded 99.95%.

Cloud infrastructure costs for the project’s sandboxes were about 80% lower than running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to let each sandbox’s memory allocation grow and shrink with its actual usage, allowing more sandboxes to share each machine.

Download DaisyRose-27B, follow the SGLang serving guide, or use Miles to train your own agents.

We’d like to hear how DaisyRose-27B performs on your tasks, including where it falls short. Share your setup and results in the model’s Community tab.

We thank Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, along with other open-source projects including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor.

#9978. Pi.dev Review 2026: A Minimalist Terminal Coding Harness

Posted on Nov 21 • Originally published at pikvue.com

Pi.dev Review 2026 — is this minimalist terminal coding harness worth trying? The verdict: yes for specific workflows, but it is not for everyone. This review covers features, pricing, performance, and how it stacks up against browser-based and cloud IDE alternatives. Here is what you need to know.

Pi.dev is a terminal-based AI coding assistant that takes a minimalist, no-nonsense approach. Instead of full IDE integration like Cursor or GitHub Copilot, Pi.dev runs directly in your terminal, understands your codebase via context files, and helps with targeted coding tasks — all without ever leaving the command line. Think of it as an AI pair programmer that lives in your shell, ready to help the moment you type a command, but never intrusive when you don't need it.

Pi.dev's core belief is that your terminal is already your most powerful tool. Don't replace it — augment it. Pi.dev doesn't try to be an IDE. It doesn't open panels, sidebars, or split views. It doesn't consume 500 MB of memory just to sit idle. It's a conversation in your terminal that can read and write files, run shell commands, reason about code architecture, and even refactor across your entire project — all from a single command-line interface.

This philosophy resonates especially well with experienced developers who have already built efficient terminal workflows and simply want AI assistance injected into their existing toolchain, not a whole new environment to learn.

To help you decide which tool fits your workflow, here's a head-to-head comparison across four major platforms for AI-assisted development.

Key takeaways: Pi.dev excels where latency, resource efficiency, and terminal-native workflows matter most. Replit offers the lowest barrier to entry with its browser-based multiplayer environment. GitHub Codespaces provides the most complete IDE experience with seamless GitHub integration. Coder is best for organizations that need to standardize development environments at scale. Each tool has a distinct sweet spot — choose based on your workflow, not hype.

Pi.dev shines in rapid prototyping scenarios. Describe what you want — "Build a FastAPI endpoint that accepts JSON payloads and stores them in SQLite" — and Pi.dev generates the complete file in seconds. Iteration is fast: you can refine the output with natural language follow-ups. The lack of IDE overhead means you go from idea to working code faster than opening a new project in VS Code. For solo developers exploring ideas, Pi.dev's speed-to-first-edit is unmatched. It helps you test a hypothesis in minutes, not hours.

While Pi.dev wasn't designed as a teaching tool, it works surprisingly well for learning. Beginners can ask "Explain this function line by line" or "Why does this code fail?" and get detailed, context-aware explanations. The terminal-native interface forces learners to understand the command line — a valuable skill in itself. However, complete beginners may find the lack of visual feedback challenging. Git diff visualizations and syntax highlighting are limited to what your terminal emulator provides. For intermediate developers looking to level up, Pi.dev is a powerful learning accelerator that explains concepts in the context of their own codebase.

Pi.dev's collaboration model is different from browser-based tools. Since it runs in a terminal, collaboration works through established Unix tools: tmux pair programming sessions, shared terminals via SSH, or screen sharing. This is less polished than Replit's multiplayer or VS Code's Live Share, but it's highly effective for teams already comfortable with terminal-based workflows. For remote server teams — DevOps engineers, backend developers, data scientists working on remote machines — Pi.dev's SSH-native design makes it the most natural collaboration tool because there's nothing to install on the server beyond a single binary.

This is arguably Pi.dev's killer use case. Writing Dockerfiles, crafting CI/CD pipelines, debugging Kubernetes manifests, or scripting infrastructure provisioning — all of these tasks happen in the terminal anyway. Pi.dev integrates directly into that workflow. You can ask it to "Write a multi-stage Dockerfile for this Node.js app" or "Explain what this Terraform block does" without leaving your command line. For platform engineers and SREs, Pi.dev is a force multiplier that reduces context switching between documentation, IDE, and terminal.

Because Pi.dev relies on AI model capabilities rather than language-specific tooling, it handles any programming language the underlying model supports. Python, JavaScript, Rust, Go, Haskell, Elixir — it doesn't matter. This makes Pi.dev particularly valuable for developers who work across multiple languages and don't want to configure a separate IDE or LSP for each one. One tool, one interface, unlimited languages.

Pi.dev's responsiveness varies by workload. Below is what matters in practice, based on the tool's documented architecture and typical terminal usage.

Startup time: Near-instant. Launching Pi.dev from the terminal takes roughly 0.5 seconds, compared to 30-90 seconds for a cold-start GitHub Codespace or 10-15 seconds for a fresh VS Code window. This makes Pi.dev ideal for quick ad-hoc coding sessions.

AI response latency: This depends entirely on your AI backend. With GPT-4o, first-token latency is typically 1-2 seconds for simple context; with Claude 3.5 Sonnet, it's similar. Complex codebases with large context windows add 3-5 seconds of initial processing time as Pi.dev compresses and indexes the context. Follow-up turns are faster since the conversation history is already loaded.

File operations: Reading files under 10 KB is instantaneous. Large files (1 MB+) take about 1-2 seconds due to context loading. File writes are essentially instant — Pi.dev applies changes directly to disk via diffs.

Multi-file operations: Refactoring across 5-10 files is bounded almost entirely by the model's generation speed, not by Pi.dev's internal processing — the harness assembles context and applies diffs while the model streams. On a slow provider the wait is the model's; on a fast one Pi.dev's overhead stays invisible.

SSH overhead: When running over SSH, latency is negligible for interactive use. The Pi.dev binary runs entirely on the remote machine; only text streams over the SSH connection. Even on a high-latency international link, the experience stays responsive because there's no GUI rendering to transmit — the round trip carries keystrokes and text, not frames.

Resource consumption: Pi.dev's idle memory footprint sits at 30-50 MB. During AI generation, this rises to 150-200 MB temporarily. CPU usage is minimal — essentially zero when idle, spiking briefly during file indexing. Compare this to a VS Code + Copilot setup that consumes 500 MB+ at idle and 1-2 GB with a large workspace open.

Verdict on performance: Pi.dev is the clear winner for latency-sensitive and resource-constrained environments. If you're on a low-spec machine, over a slow network connection, or simply tired of Electron eating your RAM, Pi.dev provides a snappy AI coding experience where heavier tools struggle.

Being open source with zero markup on API costs makes Pi.dev the most affordable AI coding assistant available. Heavy users spending $50-100/mo on API tokens still come out ahead compared to a $20-39/mo subscription plus API usage.

Pi.dev fills a niche that IDE-based tools simply can't reach: AI coding assistance that lives entirely in the terminal, works over SSH, and runs on any machine regardless of specs. It's not a Cursor killer — it's a different tool for a different workflow. If your daily routine involves SSH sessions, remote servers, or resource-constrained environments, Pi.dev is indispensable. If you prefer full-featured visual IDEs with inline suggestions and graphical debuggers, stick with Cursor or Copilot.

For the right user — the terminal-native developer who values speed, efficiency, and simplicity — Pi.dev is transformative. It turns any machine with a terminal into an AI-assisted development environment in under a second.

Rating: 7.5/10 — Excellent for terminal-native workflows, limited for IDE-centric developers.

#9977. Cropping 101 photos into two screens without losing the subject

Posted on Nov 21 • Originally published at bestiphoneduo.com

The iPhone Duo has two displays that don't share an aspect ratio. The inner screen is landscape, 2670x1878. The cover screen is portrait, 1398x2034. A wallpaper that looks right on one is usually wrong on the other, so every image on Best iPhone Duo ships as two separate crops plus a 4K version.

Doing that with Image.thumbnail() produced 101 wallpapers I didn't want to look at. Centre cropping a landscape photo to 1398x2034 keeps the middle strip and throws away the edges, which on a mountain lake means the horizon sits dead centre and the far ridge disappears. So the build does the crop decision itself.

For each source image, three targets. The inner screen gets 2670x1878, the 4K download gets 3840x2700, and the cover screen gets 1398x2034. Two are landscape, one is portrait, all from the same photograph.

The rule I wanted: keep the part of the image with the most detail, but don't drift so far that the frame looks accidental. Edge density is a decent proxy for "the interesting part" on landscape photos — a treeline, a skyline, a ridge.

Downscale to 320px wide, convert to greyscale, run an edge filter, then sum edge pixels into a 1D profile along the axis being cropped:

That gives you a column profile for horizontal crops and a row profile for vertical ones. Then slide a window the width of the crop across the profile and take the one with the most energy:

The prefer term is the part that matters. Pure max-energy cropping chases a bright sky or a busy foreground and produces frames where the subject is jammed against one edge. Multiplying the score by a penalty on distance from a target centre pulls it back. For the inner screen that target is 0.5, dead centre. For the cover screen it's 0.42, slightly toward the top, because the bottom of that screen sits under the camera cutout on a lot of shots.

Two constants, and the crops stopped looking accidental.

JPEG throughout, quality 80 for the inner screen, 82 for the cover, 72 for 4K, progressive and optimised. 101 photographs come to 277MB total, which only works because each file is served immutable for a year and the grid only ever loads the thumbnails.

The accent colour for each card comes from the same resized image — a 24x24 average, no extra pass over the full-size file.

It's not a face-aware crop. On a photo where the subject is small and off-centre, edge energy can prefer a detailed background over the person. Two of the 101 needed manual offsets, which is the honest ratio for a heuristic this small.

The photos themselves are Creative Commons from Wikimedia Commons, mostly CC BY 4.0, credited to the photographer on each wallpaper page. The gallery is at bestiphoneduo.com if you want to see how the two crops sit next to each other.
